content.title: About
content.content: Mushrooms are edible fruiting bodies of fungi that are widely used in cooking. Cooked mushrooms (NS) are a ready‑to‑eat product obtained by heat treatment, preserving most nutrients and their characteristic aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Mushrooms belong to a separate kingdom of living organisms – the fungal kingdom.
Cooked mushrooms are a staple in Asian cuisine, especially in soups and stews.
Mushrooms can accumulate vitamin D when exposed to ultraviolet light.
There are over 10,000 edible mushroom species, but commercially cultivated button mushrooms and oyster mushrooms dominate the market.
Mushrooms can be grown in controlled environments, making them available year‑round.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Cooked mushrooms provide about 3 g of protein per 100 g, making them a good source of plant‑based protein.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: A cup of cooked mushrooms (≈100 g) contains only about 22 kcal, suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Mushrooms contain niacin, riboflavin, and vitamin B6, which are essential for metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Cooked mushrooms provide selenium, potassium, and copper, supporting immune function and nervous system health.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: The fiber in mushrooms aids digestive health and promotes a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to mushrooms, manifested as skin rashes or swelling.

items.title: Digestive issues
items.content: Mushrooms contain chitin, which in large amounts can cause discomfort for people with sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Improper storage can lead to bacterial or mold growth; only consume fresh or properly preserved mushrooms.

items.title: Purine content
items.content: Mushrooms are relatively high in purines, so people with gout should limit their intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked mushrooms can be added to soups, sauces, salads, pasta, and omelets. They are also used as a topping for pies and pizza. For extra flavor, briefly sauté them before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked mushrooms in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months. Discard any mushrooms with off‑odors or discoloration.
